newsitem.title: UK: Pregnant Irish prisoner to fight British election.
newsitem.headline: Pregnant Irish prisoner to fight British election.

text.p: Roisin McAliskey, a pregnant Irishwoman held in England while Germany tries to extradite her for questioning about an IRA attack, plans to protest her detention by running in Britain's May 1 general election, her mother said on Thursday.

Bernadette McAliskey, who herself held the Mid-Ulster constituency seat as a radical Roman Catholic nationalist from 1969 to 1974, said her 25-year-old daughter would stand as an independent to highlight her plight and to try to have her baby born in freedom.

But her hopes of victory suffered a setback when the main Catholic SDLP group rejected the mother's plea for the SDLP and its Sinn Fein rival to withdraw from the constituency race. Mid-Ulster is one of 18 Northern Irish seats in Britain's 651-seat House of Commons (lower house) and it is currently held by a Protestant politician.

Accusing Britain of anti-Irish racism by refusing bail to Roisin, who is eight months' pregnant, Bernadette McAliskey said the election bid "may be her only opportunity to secure her release before the birth of her child".
Later she told BBC radio: "What we have done today is set out our honest and real position on the single issue, and for this election only, (that) we may need this seat."

In 1969 Bernadette McAliskey, under her maiden name Devlin, caused a sensation when she won the same seat at the age of 22. She became the youngest woman ever elected to the British parliament but lost the seat in the 1974 general election.

Roisin McAliskey is at present in London's Holloway prison pending extradition to Germany for questioning about an Irish Republican Army (IRA) attack on a British military base at Osnabrueck last year. She denies being involved in it.
Her detention has been widely criticised by the Irish government and by Catholic politicians.
Bernadette McAliskey said that if her daughter were to be granted bail by April 16, the date when candidates must submit their names for election, "then the situation would obviously change".

Roisin plans to stand in the Mid-Ulster constituency, where she lives, if she is not given bailed before the birth. "On nomination day, if Roisin is in prison, that seat will be needed to get her out," her mother said. Britain's Home Office (interior ministry) said it was unclear whether Roisin would be released if she was nominated as a candidate.
Electoral law only states people cannot stand as candidates if they are imprisoned for more than 12 months.

A spokesman for the moderate Social Democratic and Labour Party said its candidate would not withdraw. It was critical for voters to be given the opportunity to express their views on wider political issues, the spokesman said.

Sinn Fein, the political arm of the outlawed Irish Republican Army which is fighting to oust Britain and unite the province with Catholic Ireland, reacted cautiously suggesting three-way talks with the prisoner's family and the SDLP.

"Of course the SDLP's attitude will have a direct bearing on Sinn Fein's decision," said Sinn Fein's Northern Ireland chairman Gearoid O'Hara. Protestant "Unionist" parties, representing the 60 per cent pro-British majority, traditionally win most of the seats in the province.

The SDLP recently rejected Sinn Fein overtures for electoral pacts. Sinn Fein said a joint strategy at the polls could lead to eight seats for Catholics, twice as many as now, but the SDLP said the IRA must first abandon a violent campaign which has escalated since December.
